strDesc: The case is finished in a dark matte. Its only deformities are a seam and an embossed Renbao logo in one corner. The seam opens at a touch. The two halves separate like bookcovers, angling out and down to rest on the surface below. One half holds a white shell with the shape of a brain, a hardened plastic layer which nevertheless seems flimsy, unfit for purpose. An electrician's nightmare of cables connect to the shell's upper hemisphere, flowing out like hair and disappearing into the housing below. Cables, 'tubes' really, plug into the shell at the base, presumably to deliver slurries of oxygen and sugar, and whatever else human brains need to subsist. Besides the obvious comparison (shaped as it is like the brain inside), the shell brings to mind ancient marine life, the first trilobite to venture from the sea to the land. The little telltale LEDs going on-off - its eyes blinking in the sunlight. The case hums, and glugs whenever an internal reservoir resettles. The other half of the unfolded braincase is a hollow depression, a resting place for the shell. Underneath it there are finely printed instructions in ten languages. They outline emergency care for someone untrained in the case's handling. The parts you can read mostly say to find someone who is trained in its handling, but there seems to be detail enough for you to operate it in a pinch.

strTitle: Make contact with the brain inside
strDesc:
The case is compatible with an off-the-shelf Renbao induction rig, a simple mesh of electrodes you slip over your head like a balaclava. It's an effort of will to ignore the background noise of the ship, the ambient warmth of your body, the occasional brush of clothes on your skin - an effort that, once made, becomes thoughtless, instinctive. The red-brown interior of your eyelids is overwritten with purer black, and after a moment, the Renbao logo.

"Hello?" you speak into the void of the operating system. "Testing, testing, hello." You become aware of your own avatar, and that you inhabit it: a 3D model with a poor quality scan of your own face, and a skeletal body mesh roughly based on your own proportions. You note the fine hairs on your arms, which your real body happens to lack - the exhausting reality of default settings catering to Earthers. "Mr Choong? Ben?"

No one joins you to contemplate the slowly orbiting Renbao logo. You rip off the electrodes. Briefly two realities jostle for primacy in the same v-buffer, black squares checkboarding the ship wall. You consult the manual, a dogeared booklet that fell out of the braincase lid. O-kay. Apparently there's a complicated process to setup a digital handshake between the braincase and your rig, and a troubleshooting appendix three times longer than the instructions themselves. You sigh, and get to work.

It's a less painful solve than it might have been. It takes fifteen minutes, split between puzzling out incantations for the command line, and risking a headache every time you need to quickly switch between the rig and the manual. At two separate junctures, you're convinced that there's a fundamental hardware mismatch and no amount of trial and error will solve it. Experienced spacer that you are, wunderkind troubleshooter of hardware and software alike, you push past these moments because you have no other choice. You double and triple-check the final command: rbc do let ports1n proxok handshake || cat<< "Hello?"

The black runs. Patches of near-black reveal themselves, dripping like slime down a wall. Traces of white knit together. The void becomes falling snow.

A log cabin swims into focus from out of the dark, windows dimly lit. It's cold, the air sharp on an in-breath. You start shivering.

An Asian man in his fifties leans against a door jamb, smoking a cigarette, firelight at his back. He sports a classic bowl cut, his fringe a perfect line across his forehead. "Ben Choong?" you gasp, the question mangled by cold sneaking past your lips and into your lungs.

"Speaking," he says. "What is it now?"

"Ah - it, ah -" the sensory overload precludes speech. You hug yourself for warmth, aware that your real body is perfectly temperate. This body you're also in has other ideas.

Choong looks as if he is trying hard not to roll his eyes at you. "You'd better come inside," he says. When your legs threaten to fail you, he loops an arm under yours and assists you across the threshold.

"I don't have time for this," you say, warm enough to trust your tongue again. "Ben Choong. I need your help."

He visibly recalibrates. "That's a first," he says. "I don't see how I could possibly help anyone. Every secret I've ever known, I've divulged. Every confidence betrayed. There's nothing more you people can take from me."

You infer his meaning, though it takes a second. "I'm not here to interrogate you," you say slowly. "I think we may need to start over. I found you - your brain - " What even is the situation? How to describe your current relationship? "I'm ... taking care of it, for the moment. Whatever I can do for you, I will. But I need your help. You have information vital to the war effort." The cliched line rolls off your tongue like a cheap knockoff on a factory line, all the more unsatisfying that it happens to be true.

Choong can't hide the glimmer of hope that sparks in his eyes. It dies immediately, doused in pessimism. "Ridiculous," he says. "I truly don't know what you think this will wheedle out of me. It's a poor effort, a threadbare deception."

"My name is [us-fullname]." You try to project sincerity. Strange that it doesn't come naturally. "I'm [us-age] years old. I'm from [us-homeworld]. I'm a ship captain."

"I'm nothing more than a brain in a jar; I have no way to verify anything you tell me," says Ben Choong. "How can you expect me to believe anything you say?"

He begins without any more prompting. His words are confident, but hasty. He seems to have gone over this history many times before, enough to have an answer prepared and ready.

"I was born on Earth," he says, "which I don't remember at all. I was shipped up the beanstalk to Luna when I was a child, with my parents, who worked on a base. I have one memory of Earth: riding in the back seat of a car when it was raining. I remember the red lights of the cars ahead shimmering through the windshield."

This image doesn't coalesce for you - a shield for wind? - before he moves on. "My parents died when I was young, a few years apart, and I became the property of a BNW creche. I excelled in school, mostly in humanities, and got the grades to enter Voltaire University. I was a terrible rego miner," he says, grinning shamefacedly. "The creche was happy to see the back of me. I studied, graduated, was rewarded with a bunch of important letters after my name."

"Pretend I don't know anything about what you've done," you say. "What was so important about your research?"

He nods gamely, as if he's heard this exact 'clean-slate, start-from-the-start' line of questioning before. "There is a substance," he says, "and don't ask me anything about it because I swear I can't answer the technicalities. But it has exotic properties of some kind. I don't understand them. It's magic rock, to someone like me. And it exists in our solar system."

"The Belters called it 'void opal', because in solid form it's opalescent, and - you get it. I suppose I'm directly responsible for alerting the powers-that-be to its existence. That's the short version." He looks at you for encouragement, sees incomprehension, and starts on the medium length version.

"When I was living with the Belters - I lived with many tribes, but the one in question called themselves New Colchis - I discovered they had a secret. Not by design, but in practice. They simply didn't talk to outsiders about it, and traded with Inners for air and water without ever bringing it up. I'm sure they would've happily told anyone, had anyone thought to ask."

strTitle: Ask why this was done to him
strDesc:
"Your research into the Belters," you say. "Was that how you wound up in ... in your situation?"

"As an excavated brain, you mean?" He enjoys your discomfort. He must have had time to come to terms with his existential lot.

"Yes," you say. "Your situation."

"To tell you the truth, I can only speculate," he says. He cocks his head. "You could jack out and ask your handlers, who would have a better idea than me."
Dr. Choong waits expectantly for your question.

"What do you know," you say, unable to keep the gravitas out of your voice, "about VHS?"

"Literally nothing," he says. "What are you talking about?"

"Videotapes. Cassettes. Little black boxes full of film." Your questions reach further as his expression fails to comprehend.

"Can I use a search engine?" he asks, a touch afraid, as if fearing the consequences for not knowing.

You sigh. "Go ahead."

He conjures a window at his eye level and dutifully inputs 'VHS'. He scrolls past images, text descriptions, analysis. "I think I've seen this before," he says, tapping and enlarging one of the simpler images.

A hopeful note: "You have?"

"Sometimes it's used as a save icon instead of a disk," he says, relieved. "Yes, I've definitely seen it used as a save icon."

Frustration has you pinch the bridge of your nose, both in this reality and the one previous.

strTitle: Speculate the tapes were made for Choong
strDesc:
"I'm left wondering why someone made the tapes. Were they a personal attack on you? Did you know anyone, was there anyone in your life, with some kind of vendetta against you?"

"Let me see," Choong says blithely, "besides whoever tortured me to death, resurrected me, and continued to torture me in a cheap digital afterlife? No, nobody springs to mind."

strTitle: Speculate the tapes were made by God, or an alien
strDesc: "I had hoped talking to you would clear this up," you say, realising there are no easy answers forthcoming. "But I have more questions than I started with. The tapes have no providence." Choong looks unsympathetic, and doesn't reply. You muse further. "Providence, I suppose, is what it's all about. Did your religious Belters ever get up to something like this? Or their deity? Did it ever tell them, 'I will make cryptic videotapes, yea, and verily will I seed them in a cosmic junkyard?'" Your joking tone glances off Choong. "Their relationship with their God was personal," he says, "and they wouldn't discuss what He said to them with one another, much less me."

strTitle: Speculate the tapes were made by military intelligence
strDesc:
"Whoever had access to your footage would have been the same people who got you the first time," you say. "That much is clear. Xinhua, I assume."

"It makes sense," he says. "I was abducted on Luna, and despite the Lunar-Martian split there's some trace loyalty remaining. Believe it or not, I saw exceedingly few people in all that time. The people I did see may well have been Xinhuan."

"It doesn't make sense," you break in, "because why would they make it at all?"

"You're too far ahead," he says. "Xinhua needn't have made anything. Sensitive information is traded, lost, hacked, leaked, stolen, all the time. Xinhua in particular is vulnerable to bribery. Someone else could've got their hands on it. A defector, maybe, who went from Xinhua to the CIA on Titan."

"It doesn't make any sense for Titan to have made it, either," you say stubbornly.

"You have the right of it," he agrees.
Dr. Choong waits expectantly for your next question.

strTitle: Ask him if he knows Smiley
strDesc: "Have you ever been to K-Leg? Did you ever meet anyone from the AV Club?" "No, and no." "And you've never met anyone calling themselves Smiley," you say flatly, "who had a penchant for disguising themselves." "I've never met anyone going by that name," he agrees, "and if someone were disguising themselves, I don't see how I'd know that." Once again Choong looks around at the pseudo virtual environment you share, as if testing its authenticity. "In my situation, as you call it, I'm doubly incapable. For all I know, you are Smiley. For all you know, I am Smiley." "Maybe we're both Smiley," you say acidly. Was he this much a pedant before he became a software emulation? "We've both forgotten our true identities, and we're chasing our tail in circles." "It sounds insane, yes." Ben smiles. Luckily, you detect none of the superior know-it-all-ness in his expression that you've come to dread. "But that's the kind of insane thing this Smiley character might do, based on what you've told me." "I'm going to move on from this line of inquiry." "By all means."

strTitle: Ask him about the military applications
strDesc: "You said before that the New Colchians had discovered something the military wanted," you say. "What was it?" Choong blinks. He has a distinctive blink, both eyes really hard at once. "I'd have thought that was obvious, if you're familiar with my footage." "Clean slate rules," you remind him. "No stupid questions." "Fine," he says, "but only if you accept stupid answers in kind. That being, the answer is teleportation." "Teleportation." "From my lips to God's ears," he insists, "without passing through an intervening medium. You saw the video, didn't you? Girl goes in, door closes, machine hums, door opens, no more girl. Where is she? Somewhere else. Quod erat demonstrandum." "It was real?" "Of course it was real," he says impatiently, "or you wouldn't be here, and more importantly, I wouldn't be here." "It's not possible," you say. Choong looks at you. "It's not physically possible." "Then we're done. Can I go home?" he asks darkly. "Put me in a new body, make me the world's first total body transplant."

"Teleportation, though," you repeat. "How does it work? Doesn't it violate relativity? Causality?"

"I don't know," he says slowly, as if to a slow-witted child. "I'm an anthropologist, not a theoretical physicist."

"It violates common sense."

"Oh, absolutely," he agrees. "Along with the God-rock, it's the single most important discovery in recorded history. It demands a reassessment of common sense itself."

"Occam's razor, then," you say. "It must be a hoax."

Choong eyes you, as would a teacher to a precocious student overstepping. "Put that away, you'll hurt yourself." He puts up a hand, forestalling any more on the subject. "I don't care to talk about this. I've been over it more times than I can count. My best guess is, they discovered functional teleportation. Take it or leave it. If you're of a mind to do it already, send me to the pain room."

strTitle: Ask about the destination of the teleportation
strDesc: "When this Belter girl went into the sarcophagus," you ask, testing the structural limit of a dubious addition to your reality, "where did she come out?" "No idea," Choong says promptly. "So how do you -," "- know that it was teleportation?" Choong mimics your question. Seems he's heard it before. "I don't. It's an article of faith. However you slice it, if she wasn't in that box, by definition, she teleported out of it." "I suppose the Colchians claimed she went to Heaven," you say. "Her name was Ketevan," he says mildly, "and no, they didn't. There was no Heaven in their theology. Common in modern religion - Gods, yes. Hell, of course. Heaven, no. A world full of cynics has no time for Heaven." "Then where?" "They said, and this was the entire point of the exercise," he says, with the air of someone reciting a flimsy pretext, "that Keti had gone to God. That she was one with God. Transubstantiation, if you like, rather than teleportation." "They sent that poor girl to join with God?" "Yes, and many others," he says. "Anyone who wanted to go, really."

"They volunteered to get into an eldritch sarcophagus," you say. "They wanted to become one with God."

"Wouldn't you?" he shoots back. Something tells you his heart isn't in it. "Consider it. I don't know your religion - I could make an educated guess, but I won't - but you must understand why they'd do it, even if you're not religious. Consider the hypothetical from first principles. God is real, the Creator of our Universe, and He offers you the choice to become One With Him. Assume that entails immortality, omniscience, changing your participation in reality from that of a mortal subject to that of a supernatural force. Would you say yes?"

"I've never been a God before," you say. "I don't know if I'd like it. Did He offer a trial period, a try-before-you-buy?"

"Religion is never big on guarantee, as a rule," he says. "Most of them make a virtue out of it."

"I would at least consider it," he says, "and I'm as atheistic as they come. On the other hand, the Belters were a young community cut off from the rest of their species, further altered by an exotic psychoactive agent. For them it was a no-brainer. They were happy to do it. It was a joyous occasion." 

No, his heart definitely isn't in it. He's arguing for the sake of it, because he can't help but pitch in for the opposite view.

"There's no way in hell I'm taking that deal without knowing more," you say. "Be God? It could mean literally anything."

"For some, I can imagine that being a plus," he says. "Not everyone is happy with their lot."

"Tell me about Ketevan," you say, "the girl who became one with God."

"What about her?" he asks politely.

If there is a reason this man has been tortured to death and back, it is surely this, you reflect. For it is obvious that he is preparing to become evasive, preparing to deceive, even if he has tried and failed time and time before. Though represented by this software-dream projection of his body, he cannot help but send unconscious signals through it.

What a tragedy for Dr. Benjamin Choong, that he be born a terrible liar.

"How did you meet?"

"Probably in a refectory," he says, squinting, "The main social hubs, shared eating spaces, that kind of thing."

"You knew each other."

"Oh, in a sense," he says, "by sight. We saw each other around. You got to know everyone in those tight-knit communities."

"You knew her by sight," you repeat. "So what, you invented the name 'Ketevan'?"

"I knew her name." He stares at the table between you. "I knew everyone's name. I'm good with names."

"An academic, good with names," you say drily. "What's my name, Ben? I told you right after we met."

He opens his mouth. And shuts it again. His gaze is squarely down.

"I'm [us-fullname]. I'm a ship captain from K-LEG. I'm not your jailer."

He chooses not to reply, nor to look up.

strTitle: Tell him he's lying about Ketevan
strDesc: "I think you're lying to me," you say, "about this woman. I don't know how exactly." "Do your worst," he says. The words are defiant, even though they come from a man who could be reasonably mistaken for a ghost. You stand up and walk to the fire. Stretching your legs helps to think, though of course it also reminds you that your legs are curled beneath you on the floor of your ship. "Is this a lie you've told before?" you ask him. No reply. "I can't imagine I'm the first person to realise that," you say to the fire. A log shifts a little, and it sparks eagerly. "You must have clammed up, and they would have pressured you." The fire is much more interested in your ideas than Ben. "Did you break?" you say to the man, silent and still in his chair. "Have you already broken? How many times? And why try it to keep silent, even now?" He says nothing. "It's -" you catch yourself, a sentence halfway out the door. It's going to be easier if you're honest with me. A cliche straight out of a movie. But that's the difficulty. What can you tell this man? There's no point lying. Look where you are. I'm actually on your side! All these cliches had sounded farcical until this very second, now that they are bizarrely applicable; and cliches are all you have, because you have not the first idea how to talk to a prisoner, how to get them to reveal what they know, how to win their trust. That's the trouble. He expects that you're going to start torturing him yourself, and if he really doesn't believe you, what will you do?

"I want to know more about Ketevan," you say plainly. "Because you don't want to tell me."

He quirks his eyebrows, saying nothing. A mute parry - 'good for you'.

"She's the sole Belter you've named. She must've been important."

No reply.

"Important to you, perhaps."

No reply.

"Maybe you were in love."

No reply.

"Under the surface, I'll bet you're a romantic at heart."

No reply.

"Are researchers supposed to fall in love with their subjects?"

No reply, but a palpable hit: he's affronted, angry.

strTitle: Hone in on the problematic angle
strDesc:
"No, probably not. That would've been an ethical dilemma."

No reply. He looks away, brimming with murderous anger.

"Especially since you were a fancypants academic, pulled himself up by his bootstraps, smartest kid in creche, and she was a dumb-as-rocks tribal gaga for God."

His body jerks, hands flexing, as if compelled to leap up and throttle you to death. The impulse has been carefully trained out of him.

At last he speaks, jaw visibly clenched. "Do you have a point?"

You shake your head. "Stop me if I get one wrong," you say.

"Your captors," you say, "who I stress are not me, we're not associated, I'm itinerant. What did they do to you?"

Choong is shocked out of silence. "You want me to explain how I was tortured? Are you fucking kidding?"

"No, no," you say. He's so uncharitable. "I was just curious!"

"If you really are 'just' curious," he says, "I think it shows unbelievably poor taste. And if not, read the fucking manual."

There probably are relevant instructions in the manual.

"Maybe it would help if I convinced you I'm on the level," you say. "That I am who I say I am."

"I'm listening," he says.

You tell him about K-LEG, the little asteroid in the middle of nowhere. Growing up in the shadow of the shipbreaker's yard, learning from the get-go that your value was pretty much in direct proportion to your facility with your tools. Looking at the dot of Old Earth, another colourful dot in the starry sea, and wondering how clear water could turn it blue.

At some point you lose track of your own story. It becomes a confusing sequence of ships, people, and spacefaring minutiae. "... that's about it." He nods seriously.

"Come on," you say, "would a spy really make up all of that just to appear trustworthy?"

He shakes his head. "It's tautological. A spy would have to make up something to appear trustworthy, such as all that, and more."

"Help me out," you say. "What could I say to get you to trust me?"

"You don't understand," he says. "You truly don't. No matter what you say, I have to distrust it. Even if it sounds true, even if it would be convenient, even if I'd want it to be true very very much, formally speaking, I can't believe anything you say because you have complete control over my perception of reality. Look up the 'Cartesian demon', if you like."

Incredible: he's actually prescribing secondary reading. You can take the man out of the university ... "But I'm not doing that!" you say. "I'm not tricking you."

"And I want that to be true," he says sadly. "I really do. For what it's worth, you've led quite an interesting life. I hope it's turning out how you wanted."
Dr. Choong waits expectantly for your next question.

strTitle: Alert Choong to the stakes viz a viz: war
strDesc:
"You need to know what we're up against," you say. "The Great Powers are on the eve of open warfare."

"No," he says, "the Great Powers would never."

"This is important," you say impatiently. "I'm serious."

"You look serious." He makes a visible effort to tolerate it. "Fine. Say what you have to say."

You give a rundown of the deteriorating situation between Ceres and Jupiter, seasoned with a few personal anecdotes you've experienced along the way. Ceres being overrun with agents of dubious loyalty. Ships disappearing. Military buildups reported around Mars and Saturn.

"Ceres might try to repeat the attack on Ganymede, or worse, an attack on Titan. Titan could demolish Ring Station without a second thought. Xinhua and the US are being drawn into open conflict with one another. It's all bad."

"This is nothing new," says Choong calmly. "In fact, it's right on schedule."

strTitle: Demand to know what schedule he's referring to
strDesc: "'On schedule?'" you repeat. "You knew this was coming?" "Yes," he says. "This war in potentia has been modelled in detail since the 50s. It should've happened sooner, but we got lucky." "You can model a war?" Choong raises a hand again, an annoying habit of his. "It's settled, in the academic community, that the System is in decline. Terminal decline. The writing's been on the wall since we lost Earth." A cold chill creeps down the back of your neck. He sounds so confident, so calm, completely at odds with the terrifying sentiment. Haunting his words is a spectre of decades of furious, desperate debate, and all that has been collated, synthesised, and presented as fact. You swallow. "You sound like a doomer on a social feed," you say. They're a dime a dozen. He both nods and shakes his head, a noncommittal back-and-forth. "I'm sure plenty of them are former colleagues. BNW didn't like the idea. If your paper wasn't happy enough they'd blackball you. Then you had plenty of free time to argue with OSINT nutters." "So they're right? What do you mean, decline?" Choong blinks his distinctive both-eyed blink, like a genteel reptilian. "I mean in every field of academic inquiry, in every way we organise our social critique, we see that the building blocks to keep a human alive in space are disappearing." He holds up a hand and checks off his fingers. "Food, water, oxygen. Our breadbaskets aren't producing enough food. Our volatiles aren't processed with enough speed. Medicine, the amount of novel ailments discovered in colonisation aren't even properly categorised, let alone understood. Security, society, all fragmenting. Two superpowers are tooling up to decide who's king of a bunch of rocks. They needn't bother. Famine will do their work all the quicker." "Uh huh," you say, the dutiful skeptic. "So how long have we got? Ten years? Five?" Choong purses his lips. "What's today's date?" You tell him. He does a quick calculation in his head. "Six months." "Six?!" you all-but choke on the word. "Six if we're being optimistic. Our subsistence - excuse me, our means of producing life-sustaining goods - barely contributed to a vast reserve banked from Earth. From the second they went up, to the days they came tumbling down, the Earth elevators worked day and night ferrying us food and water and people and oxygen and, you get the picture, for twenty years. Twenty. Years. It was our cornucopia, our horn of plenty. We were profligate with it. No one expected -" he swallows. He blinks and moves on. "Since then, our consumption has always been a considerable net negative. You can't really expect a handful of Quonset huts on Titan or Mars to provide for all the millions exiled from the garden of Eden. Offworld industries are, always were, paper tigers; propaganda. Once our Earth surplus runs out, well ..." "You, you ..." You struggle for a rejoinder. He waits patiently, a sad little smile on his face. "... you can't be serious." Is that the best you've got? It's the best you've got. "It's like I said," he continues, unperturbed. "We lost Mother Earth." Mother Earth, you note, not Old Earth, like the System brands it. "Oh, the effort out here has been valiant, admirable in its own way - our tangle of outposts, colonies - some of those Martian films weren't half bad - but our number is up."

strTitle: Ask how the end will come
strDesc:
"What will happen in six months?" you ask. "When we run out of supplies. We starve?"

"No," he says. "The war will come sooner than that. With it, new emergency powers, reorganisation of the economy. Rationing. They will stretch out the reserves as long as they can. The war will touch everyone, everything, and steadily reduce the scope of the problem - fewer mouths eat less. That will buy another few years for the victor."

"And then?"

"The wartime footing will never be relaxed, even without an opponent," he says, rubbing his temple. "Nor will the rationing. They will try to redirect public attention to the vanishing remnants of the loser, but we would expect central authority to degrade further. No matter how repressive a ruler gets, they cannot control a starving populace."

"And then?"

"Solar trade, already disrupted by the war, will cease, and the tenuous cultural identities of the United States and/or Xinhua will dissolve completely, replaced by frightened regional authorities. A bit like K-LEG," he adds. "Everywhere will become K-LEG. A tiny fiefdom ruled by a despot."

"And then?"

"And then we starve," he says. "One by one, our little lights in the darkness will flicker out."

"There must be something we can do," you say. "That someone can do. Things can't end."

"You pretend that they won't," Choong says, false and bright. "And do what you were going to do anyway. After all, human civilisation has never ended before. It's crazy to think that it would now."

"That's it?" you say incredulously. "Embrace fatalism?"

"I did my best to move the social needle," he says. "Look what happened to me."

"The golden sarcophagus," you say. "What was it?"

"A human effigy," he says, warming to the subject. "Their idol, an object of worship."

"And a mode of transport."

"I doubt we'll ever see its like in a secondhand dealership," he says drily, "but yes. That also."

"Where did it come from?" you ask eagerly. "They didn't find it buried in an asteroid too, did they?"

"I expect, given the negative phrasing, you thought I'd make fun of you for proposing something so absurd," he says.

"It crossed my mind."

"Well, I apologise for giving you that impression," he says with sincerity. "I think it's a very good question, with a complicated answer."

"So ... did they?"

"No. They made it themselves." He smiles, enjoying some private joke. "But after what I've told you about the hallucinogenic substance, it's not so unreasonable to imagine aliens secreting mystical artefacts across our solar system. Perhaps on Earth, too, at Giza, or Palenque."

You fight back a sigh. "Does it get more complicated than that?"

"Yes, it does," he continues. "I believe the idea for the sarcophagus was conceived through that shared hallucination. They built it, yes, but it was a colossal undertaking, not the whim of one leader or priest, and certainly not the product of one man's labour."

"A fab on Titan or Mars could spin that up in a day or two," you say, on solid ground for once. "And most of that time budget would be spent in CAD."

"A valid argument, but not sound," he says, and he's terribly happy to say it. "You're missing something. The entire piece was gold."

"Gold gold?"

"Gold gold," he confirms. "Elemental gold."

Three thousand years ago, that was an irresponsible allocation of resources. It still is today. "Why?"

"I have no idea!" He's overjoyed with the mystery. "It's something I've always wondered about. It took them months to find a sufficiently rich asteroid, explore it, and extract what they needed, all the while continuing to meet obligations to their creditors. The project might have bankrupted them, especially without a return."

It was always natural to assume it simply had a gold exterior, not that it was totally composed of the metal. "It was their vessel for teleportation," you say. "Perhaps that was why."

"I'm a layman metallurgist," he says, "but I'm certain that gold alone doesn't confer the power of teleportation."

strTitle: Ask if the Colchian God is an extraterrestrial
strDesc:
"Do you think it's aliens, then?" No point beating around the bush. "Instead of secreting artefacts throughout the system, they secreted their magic rock around the place. Same difference."

Choong leans back in his chair, and stares at the ceiling. He interlocks his fingers, and for a moment, says nothing, deep in thought. "... Dr. Choong?" you ask, after a while.

"Sorry," he says, blinking and returning to the present. "It's a question I've turned over in my mind for a long time. Decades. My considered opinion: ascribing extraterrestrial means to the New Colchians' actions does go a long way to explaining how unlikely they are, but, well," he sticks a finger in his ear, somehow contriving it to be thoughtful. "I think it merely kicks the can down the road."

"Meaning?"

"It delays real answers."

"Right."

"But," you say, "they say their God talked to them. They developed a working teleportation device. That's not by random chance. How could an alien not be behind it?"

"An alien could be behind it," he says, and in his voice you can hear the pedagogic gears begin to turn. "It simply doesn't answer anything important, like why it would tell them to do it, or how. We can't see this alien of yours," he says, 'of yours', as if this is your wild fancy. "We can't touch it, hear it, or observe it in any way, and we only know of it through secondhand testimony. I don't know how or why everything has happened the way it did," he says, trying to make it sound like a concession, "but, speaking metaphysically, saying 'an alien did it' is the same conclusion as 'God did it' or 'a wizard did it'. It's not important."

That's you told. You sit back, considering him, rather than his words. The teacher voice he puts on, is that something he brings out whenever he's arguing disingenuously? A persona he adopts to conceal his true feelings? It's a compelling trick, to bog you down in argumentation, but something tells you he didn't experience everything he did and come out the other side without deciding for himself one way or the other.

"You're playing games with me," you say. He looks at you levelly. It's how you might imagine the captain of an enemy ship, as you come about, revealing to their scopes an underbelly bristling with weapons running hot. Contact.

"You said you believe they've discovered a technology that contradicts all of physics," you say, resisting the urge to fidget. "Now you pretend to be disinterested in how they did it."

"Uninterested," he says automatically.

"Whatever!" you snap, wondering how things got to this point. "This phenomenon you claimed to witness, whatever it is, it's obviously supernatural. Why won't you admit that?"

"There's no such thing," he says.

"Excuse me?"

"There's no such thing as the supernatural, by definition," he says. "I don't mean to provoke you, but you have to allow me this point. 'Natural' encompasses all things that exist. 'Supernatural' describes things that do not, cannot, exist. If something exists, it is natural. If something does not exist, it is supernatural. Witnessing something and calling it supernatural is a category error, whether or not you can explain it."

More word games. "Do you believe the New Colchians discovered teleportation by accident," you say carefully, hoping to pin him with a yes-or-no. "Or not?"

He spreads his hands. "I don't know." 

This is as close as you can get to a win: you're sure that he's lying.
Dr. Choong stares, eyes empty of emotion.

You describe to him your story of finding a videotape in a derelict spaceship, drifting millions of kilometres from anywhere. He listens, nodding, not really understanding.

Finally when it comes to the videos themselves, you have a bright idea.

"Wait here," you say.

"I'm not going anywhere," he says, a shade reproachful.

"You had an illicit relationship with Ketevan," you say. "That much is clear. But why would you be embarrassed or defensive about it when it happened decades ago? Because that's just a ruse. You must have moved on. She's probably dead, or -" and how to put the alternative? You shrug. "Or an angel or something. No doubt you've tied up your interrogators in knots for years pretending to hold on to that."

He's perfectly still - which is a dead giveaway. He seems to realise it himself after a moment. He takes a deep breath, and resettles in his chair. "I don't see how it concerns you," he says, "or anyone else, for that matter. What do you want, the poetry I wrote her? A knife carving in the hull, 'B+K'?"

"You're doing it again," you say evenly, "pretending it's the love affair you're protecting." He doesn't reply, and the only sound is the howling wind.

strTitle: He's lying about the Colchians' religion
strDesc:
"I don’t believe that you don’t believe in the supernatural," you say. "However you define it. However you rationalise it. I think you know more about the Colchian God, whatever it was."

"Okay, it was an alien. Happy?" He smirks.

"Not really, no." You look in your coffee cup. It’s long been empty. Shouldn’t it refill itself automatically, in a place like this? "Your whole life has been empirical observation. A claim that contradicts physical laws isn’t something you could equivocate about: 'oh, well maybe it’s real and nobody ever figured it out’. Then you dress up the contradiction with meaningless philosophy."

"Sophistry," he supplies the word for you. Then, after a second, "which, um, isn’t something I’m doing."

"I dunno, man," you say. "You're not being honest somehow. There's a chunk missing from all of this. I can feel it. You know what it is, and you're not talking."

"I'm talking," he says, an edge of desperation to his voice, as if he's mentally preparing himself for more pain. "I'm doing nothing but."

strTitle: He's lying about the end of humanity
strDesc:
"I've never heard of this Earth surplus before today," you say. "And even if it's real, I've never seen signs it's running out."

He frowns, and shakes his head like he can't believe what he's hearing. "You grew up on a rock floating in the middle of nothing," he says viciously, accessing an untapped well of condescension. "Everything you ever ate, drank, or breathed, was shipped to you at a massive expense. You have no idea what you're talking about, no idea how tenuous your life really is."

"I'm a ship's captain now," you say proudly. "I don't need anyone for anything."

His mouth actually falls open, an expression you've read about but never seen. "You're as doomed as I am," he says, after snapping it shut.

strTitle: He's lying: he made the videotapes
strDesc:
"I don't know why, or how," you say, "but you must have made the videotapes. Perhaps to lure people to you. Perhaps as an escape attempt. After all, it worked: I'm here."

"It took me a second to remember what the hell you're talking about," he says. "This is the first I've heard about your stupid tapes. Zero marks, see me after class."

strTitle: Say you don't care if he's lying
strDesc:
"I think, in your situation," you say, "anyone could be forgiven for lying. Putting your brain in this device was cruel, and bizarre."

"No argument here," he says.

"That's all I wanted to say. Whatever your secrets may be, you're entitled to them, if nothing else."

"Forgive me," he says tonelessly. "But I couldn't care less what you think."

Choong, as it stands, seems like a dead end. He has no answers for you about the videotape mystery, nor how it interfaces with the incipient war, besides the origins at New Colchis. Whatever he's hiding, you may have to content yourself that it is beyond your reach ...

His life is in your hands, in the most literal sense.

strTitle: Torture him to see what he's hiding
strDesc:
"I'm running out of options," you say, for yourself as much as him. "The Great Powers are convinced you hold the secret to the war. Even if they're wrong, I have to try. The cost is too high."

"No," he says quietly. One pitiful little no. Even after it all, he still didn't see this coming. He wanted to believe. He had hope.

"Then tell me!" you explode. "Tell me what you're holding on to! Tell me why they did this to you!"

He closes his eyes, processing, some internal battle between release and guilt, punishment and fear.

His expression firms. He opens his eyes. "No."

You take off the rig. Blinking away the last images of Choong and the log cabin, you stretch your arms, wondering how long it's been.

The device is forthcoming about how to proceed. There are logs of prior sessions, and it's not difficult to recreate one.

The scenario they used the most is titled The Pain Room. The application byline calls it the gold standard in the field of Computer Assisted Interrogation, and has many quick setups and user guides to get you started.

Is there such a thing as morality? Is there really? 

This much is obvious to you: evil, 'immoral' things happen on the daily, everywhere, and you always hear the same line: everyone thinks they're a good person. They can't both be true - rather most of those people thinking themselves good have to be plain wrong, ipso facto. Good people do evil things, and pretend it was okay afterwards, or that it didn't happen. If it were really so wrong to hurt someone, there would be no war, and if a veteran soldier broadcasted everything they did when they returned home, they would be shunned. We keep right and wrong around when it's useful, and when it's not, we try to ignore it. You could do or say whatever you want, and never tell anyone afterward.

So why do you feel so totally averse to this? Why are your hands poised to command it to shut off?

You have justification. Primarily, he's concealing information that could decide the fate of millions. Secondarily, he's annoying. Third, or tertiarily as Choong might smugly put it, the damage has already been done, and by whole cadres of state actors from both sides, no less. Who really cares what happens to him? If you have to put anyone in something called The Pain Room, it might as well be someone who's been there plenty of times already.

Still, with all that rattling around in your head, your hands execute the command, and The Pain Room quits.

Before you torture him, you decide to torture yourself, first.

The Pain Room's readme describes a featureless room where the subject is immobilised and various parts of the brain are directly stimulated to induce pain. There are many different kinds of pain it can do. Vast swathes of grey matter are devoted to modelling damage and abrasion on every other part of the body, and all of them are fair play, each detailed in dedicated chapters. 

The skin, broad surface that it is, has many different notes to strike - cuts, boils, bruises, burns, all the way up to nasty stuff like degloving and neuropathy.

The extremities, lips, mouth, fingers, genitalia, all have trillions of nerve endings to bother, and a forest of subheadings detailing the different ways the program can do it, none of which you feel compelled to expand. 

The gut has a lengthy chapter on simulating acute inflammation, or a classic gutshot in a variety of calibers. 

Finally the notes explain the program can simply convince the prefrontal cortex it is experiencing pain on a scale of 1 to 10, and warns that above a 7 risks unconsciousness, and 9 or 10 will reliably cause a coma within seconds.

strTitle: Send Choong to the Pain Room
strDesc:
You think of all the poor souls on Mars and Titan, Venus and Ganymede, Luna and Ceres; even the handful of souls worth saving on K-LEG, who must surely exist, even if you never met any.

There's no other choice. One must suffer so the rest might not.

You context-switch Ben Choong from the Moretti Branded Experience to The Pain Room, and in he goes, a portion of water poured from one cup into another.

Nothing changes from the exterior. The brain shell does not move, and the perfusion keeps glugging away. You hear no ghostly cries of anguish.
